# Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and rationale

Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of hospitalization and death worldwide, and for decades inhibition of the renin–angiotensin system (RAS) formed the pharmacological backbone of therapy. The natriuretic peptide system represents a counter-regulatory pathway: natriuretic peptides promote vasodilation, natriuresis and diuresis, and suppress renin and aldosterone release. Natriuretic peptides increase glomerular filtration rate, resulting in natriuresis and diuresis, and reduce renin release from renal juxtaglomerular cells, thereby reducing plasma angiotensin II and subsequent aldosterone secretion, resulting in vasodilation [1]. Because these peptides are degraded by neprilysin, neprilysin inhibition became an attractive therapeutic target [1].

Early efforts combined neprilysin inhibition with ACE inhibition. Inhibiting neprilysin has been a therapeutic target for several compounds tested in cardiovascular disease, including ecadotril, candoxatril, omapatrilat, and LCZ696; however, lack of efficacy and side effects led to discontinuation of the earlier agents [1]. In the OVERTURE trial, 5770 patients with NYHA class II to IV heart failure were randomized to either enalapril (10 mg twice daily) or the ACE–neprilysin inhibitor omapatrilat (40 mg once daily) [2]. OVERTURE demonstrated that omapatrilat reduced morbidity and mortality but was not more effective than ACE inhibition alone in reducing the primary endpoint, and its development was abandoned because of angioedema risk arising from dual bradykinin inhibition [2]. The eventual solution—pairing neprilysin inhibition with an angiotensin receptor blocker rather than an ACE inhibitor—gave rise to sacubitril/valsartan (LCZ696), the first-in-class angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) [1].

## The PARADIGM-HF trial

The pivotal PARADIGM-HF trial transformed HF therapy. In this double-blind trial, 8442 patients with class II, III, or IV heart failure and an ejection fraction of 40% or less were randomly assigned to receive either LCZ696 at 200 mg twice daily or enalapril 10 mg twice daily, in addition to recommended therapy [3]. The trial was stopped prematurely after a median follow-up of 27 months on the recommendation of the data safety monitoring board owing to compelling evidence favoring sacubitril/valsartan [4]. Patients receiving sacubitril/valsartan had a reduced risk of the primary composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.73–0.87); the hazard ratio for all-cause mortality was 0.84 (95% CI 0.76–0.93) and for HF hospitalization was 0.79 (95% CI 0.71–0.89) [4]. Benefits extended to recurrent events: compared with enalapril, sacubitril/valsartan reduced both first and recurrent events, with a similar treatment effect size regardless of the statistical approach [5]. ARNI therapy also slowed disease progression—fewer LCZ696-treated patients required intensification of medical treatment for heart failure or an emergency department visit for worsening heart failure [6]. A meta-analysis pooling IMPRESS, OVERTURE and PARADIGM-HF supported the use of combined neprilysin/RAS inhibition in HF with reduced EF [7]. Even patients unable to reach target doses derived benefit: participants taking lower than target sacubitril/valsartan doses had a lower risk of the primary event compared with those taking lower than target doses of enalapril [8].

## Mechanisms and reverse remodeling

The mechanisms underlying clinical benefit have been illuminated by the PROVE-HF study. In patients with HFrEF, sacubitril-valsartan reduces NT-proBNP concentrations, but the effect on cardiac remodeling was uncertain [9]. PROVE-HF found that reduction in NT-proBNP concentration was weakly yet significantly correlated with improvements in markers of cardiac volume and function at 12 months [9]. A reduction in NT-proBNP was demonstrated at 6 months (35%) and 12 months (37%) [9]. Both the magnitude and speed of NT-proBNP reduction were associated with reverse remodeling [10]. At a molecular level, treatment with sacubitril/valsartan led to significant reductions in aldosterone, soluble ST2, matrix metalloproteinase-9 and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases-1, reflecting reduced profibrotic signaling [11].

## Acute and hospitalized heart failure

The PIONEER-HF trial addressed in-hospital initiation. PIONEER-HF was a multicenter, randomized, double-blind trial of in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan versus enalapril in patients stabilized during hospitalization for acute decompensated HF [12]. A significantly greater reduction in NT-proBNP, the primary outcome, was seen with sacubitril-valsartan, with no significant difference in worsening renal function, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [13]. The TRANSITION study complemented these findings, showing that initiation of sacubitril/valsartan in haemodynamically stabilised heart failure patients in hospital or early after discharge was feasible [14], including in de novo HF [15]. These data support earlier, in-hospital initiation of ARNI therapy [12,16].

## Beyond HFrEF: preserved ejection fraction and post-MI

In HF with preserved ejection fraction, the PARAGON-HF trial enrolled patients with an EF of 45% or higher. Sacubitril–valsartan did not result in a significantly lower rate of total hospitalizations for heart failure and death from cardiovascular causes among patients with an ejection fraction of 45% or higher [17]. The primary endpoint was narrowly missed (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.75–1.01), but subgroups with below-median LVEF and women showed apparent benefit [18]. A pooled analysis with PARAGLIDE-HF further supported a benefit in patients with mildly reduced or preserved EF [19], consistent with a continuum of benefit across the EF spectrum [20].

Following acute myocardial infarction, PARADISE-MI tested ARNI against ramipril. Patients with myocardial infarction complicated by reduced EF, pulmonary congestion, or both were randomized to sacubitril–valsartan or ramipril in addition to recommended therapy [21]. PARADISE-MI did not meet its goal; patients on sacubitril/valsartan experienced 6.7 events per 100 patient-years versus 7.4 for ramipril, a hazard ratio of 0.90 (95% CI 0.78–1.04) [21]. Exploratory analyses of total HF events were directionally favorable [22], and an echocardiographic substudy examined effects on post-infarction remodeling [23].

## Guideline recommendations

Contemporary guidelines now position ARNI as a cornerstone of HFrEF therapy. The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline replaced the 2013 guideline and its 2017 focused update [24], recommending ARNI among the four foundational drug classes for HFrEF [25]. The 2021 ESC guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of acute and chronic heart failure similarly endorse ARNI [26], with a 2023 focused update refining recommendations across the EF spectrum [27]. A key change was renaming HF with mid-range EF to HF with mildly reduced EF, reflecting that these patients may benefit from similar therapies—ACEis/ARNIs, beta-blockers and MRAs—to those with HFrEF [26]. Supporting reviews trace the scientific path to this drug class [28] and synthesize the body of ARNI clinical trial evidence [29,30].

## Conclusion

Sacubitril/valsartan represents a landmark advance in HFrEF, reducing mortality and hospitalization beyond RAS inhibition alone, with biomarker and imaging data supporting reverse cardiac remodeling. Its role is established for hospitalized and chronic HFrEF, while evidence in preserved EF and post-MI populations is more nuanced, favoring those with lower-range ejection fractions.
